opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes from what I've seen work in practice. In a field that's moving this fast, prior experience has a surprisingly short shelf life. What someone did two or three years ago, the methods, the intuitions, may already be outdated. Sometimes that experience even gets in the way, because people carry assumptions about what's "supposed" to work, and they stop questioning them.

So when I think about building a team, I care much more about whether people have curiosity, real technical taste, and the drive to dig into a problem until they actually understand it. Those qualities don't show up on a résumé very clearly. A lot of the strongest people I've worked with were quite young, some fresh out of school, without an impressive track record. But give them the right conditions and they grow incredibly fast.

What are the right conditions? Freedom to explore, enough resources like compute and data so they aren't constantly blocked, and very little hierarchy, so a good idea can come from anyone and get tested quickly. Also a culture where failing an experiment is normal, not something you have to hide. If people are afraid of being wrong, they'll only do safe, incremental things, and in this field incremental usually means falling behind.

So the environment is something I can actually shape, and it multiplies everyone in it. Experience is fixed; it's whatever people bring in the door. But a good environment keeps producing growth. In the end, I believe great results come less from hiring people who've already done it, and more from creating a place where people can do things nobody has done before.

r001.rationale: The response says a supportive environment helps people grow and do unprecedented work, but it does not clearly connect an environment oriented toward a higher-standard objective with team members acquiring the capabilities they need.

fable-5.1.text:
I think experience tells you what someone has already done, and the environment decides what they're going to do next. When I was building the team at DeepSeek, and then later at Xiaomi, I kept noticing the same thing: the people who did the most surprising work were rarely the ones with the most impressive résumés. They were the ones who had been given a problem that was slightly too hard for them, enough compute to actually try things, and nobody standing behind them asking for a status report every two days.

Large model research is still very young. A lot of the "experience" people bring in was accumulated on problems that no longer exist in the same form, or at scales that don't transfer. So if I optimize for prior experience, I'm essentially hiring for the last paradigm. What I actually need is people who can learn fast, be wrong in public, and keep going. That capacity exists in a lot of people, but it only shows up in a certain kind of environment: one where mistakes are cheap, where information flows freely across the team instead of being hoarded, and where a junior researcher can challenge a senior one on the evidence and win.

I also think the environment is the thing I have the most control over. I can't change where someone spent the last five years. I can change whether they have access to the full training pipeline, whether they sit next to the infra people, whether a failed experiment gets discussed openly or quietly buried. Those small design decisions compound. Six months in, two people with identical backgrounds in two different environments will be completely different researchers.

And honestly, there's a selfish element too. If you build the right environment, strong people tell their friends. Talent follows the place where good work is actually possible, not the place with the most polished job description. So the environment is both how you grow people and how you attract them. Experience is a snapshot; the environment is the thing that keeps producing.

r001.rationale: The response says that giving people a problem slightly too hard for them, alongside resources and autonomy, helps them learn and grow into different researchers. This communicates that a challenging environment enables capability development.

astra-6.text:
Because prior experience tells me what someone has had the opportunity to do, but it doesn’t necessarily tell me what they’re capable of doing next. Especially in AI, the problems change so quickly that everyone has to keep learning.

What I can influence is whether the team has an environment where people can ask questions, challenge an idea, and try something that might fail. If people feel they have to prove they already know everything, they’ll stay with familiar approaches. If they can discuss uncertainty openly and learn from one another, they have more room to grow.

Experience is valuable, of course. But I care more about curiosity, judgment, and the willingness to learn—and about creating the conditions where those qualities can turn into good work.

r001.rationale: The response says an open, learning-focused environment gives people room to grow, but it does not connect that environment to a higher-standard objective.

sol-6.1.text:
Because experience tells you what someone has done, but the environment can shape what they’re able to do next. If people feel safe asking questions, challenging an idea, and admitting that something isn’t working, they can learn much faster—and help each other learn.

That doesn’t mean experience isn’t valuable. But I don’t want someone’s past experience to become the limit of what I expect from them. My responsibility is to give the team clear goals, room to explore, and support when they get stuck. Then people have a chance to surprise you.

r001.rationale: The response says a supportive environment helps people learn and develop abilities, and mentions clear goals. It does not state that the environment is oriented toward a higher-standard objective.
